title: Summer grasses
hookLine: at an old battlefield Basho writes: summer grasses, all that's left of warriors' dreams (Narrow Road to the Deep North, 1689)
tomorrow: why did Basho give up his own little house to go walking?

lines: WHERE THE FARM USED TO BE.
cards: A strip mall goes up where a farm used to be, and someone in the car who remembers the barn goes quiet. Basho knew that quiet.
On his long walk through the north of Japan, he reached Hiraizumi, once the seat of a powerful family, where, tradition says, the warrior Yoshitsune and his loyal men made their last stand.
It's a story of men dying in battle, so I'll keep it gentle. When Basho arrived, the palaces were gone. There were only fields.

teach.b: Basho writes that a line from the Chinese poet Du Fu came to him: the country is ruined, yet mountains and rivers remain; spring comes to the ruined castle, and the grass is green.

He spread his hat on the ground, he says, and sat there weeping until he lost track of time. Then the poem: natsukusa ya, tsuwamonodomo ga, yume no ato. Summer grasses: all that's left of warriors' dreams.

teach.h: HE SAT ON HIS HAT AND WEPT.
teach.b: Notice the season word, summer grasses. Lush, green, alive, and growing exactly where the dreams were. Here's the teaching.
Behind the poem is the Buddhist teaching of impermanence, mujo in Japanese: everything that is made comes apart, glory included.

The old war story, The Tale of the Heike, opens on it, with a temple bell that rings of the passing of all things. But look at what Basho doesn't do. He doesn't sneer at the warriors for their vanity.
He doesn't preach. He weeps. Impermanence, in this poem, isn't a cold fact delivered from a distance.
It's grief and tenderness at once.
And the grass isn't mocking the dead. It's simply what life does next. So when a place you loved is gone, or changed past recognizing, this tradition doesn't tell you to stop caring.
It gives you a way to stand there: see the grass, remember the dream, and let both be true.

how: Visitors to Hiraizumi can see a stone carved with Basho's summer grasses poem; Japanese readers meet it in The Narrow Road to the Deep North, often read in school.

s: Basho's summer grasses poem mocks the warriors' vanity
he sat and wept there. the poem holds grief and tenderness, not scorn.
at Hiraizumi, Basho remembered a line by the Chinese poet Du Fu
the country is ruined, yet mountains and rivers remain.
in this Buddhist view, knowing all things pass means you shouldn't grieve
Basho knew impermanence and still wept. the poem makes room for both.

games.q: your parents are selling the house you grew up in. your sibling says: 'everything changes, it's just a house, get over it.' what fits Basho at Hiraizumi?
o: everything changes, and it's still right to grieve it; then see what grows next.
your sibling's right: impermanence means there's nothing to be sad about.
fight the sale: what you love should be kept from ever changing.
games.why: Basho knew mujo, impermanence, and he still sat and wept. then he saw the summer grass growing where the dreams had been.

practice: If you can, walk slowly for a minute toward something green growing over something built: grass at a curb, a weed in a crack, moss on a wall.
Then stand still, let your breath slow, and remember one place that's gone, without trying to fix the feeling.

wordCard.voice: Summer grasses: Basho's season word at Hiraizumi, green life growing where warriors' dreams once stood. Impermanence, with tears in it.

orig.note: Japanese, from Buddhist teaching: impermanence. All made things pass.

carryVoice: Your line: summer grasses. The dream is gone and the grass is here, and both are true. See you tomorrow.
